summary: The note covers the Save Our Stories (SOS) Initiative, announced September 5, 2023, a city plan to restore historic landmarks, engage youth with history, and boost cultural and economic life through events like the TimeTravels festivals. It gathers community voices, including supporters, a skeptic worried about funding, and an architect outlining a phased funding approach. It also highlights efforts to blend history with technology, such as augmented reality tours.
one_line: The city's Save Our Stories Initiative aims to restore historic landmarks, engage youth, and boost culture and local business, drawing both enthusiasm and funding concerns.
key_facts: City officials announced the Save Our Stories (SOS) Initiative on September 5, 2023 to restore and protect key historic landmarks that have fallen into disrepair.
Councilwoman Laura Enfield and a coalition of preservationists spearheaded the SOS Initiative.
Enfield said, "Our landmarks are not just relics of the past; they're repositories of stories that continue to shape our identity and future."
The initiative has earmarked funds for workshops, school outings, and interactive exhibits to connect younger generations with the city's history.
TimeTravels, a series of cultural festivals with themed weekends dedicated to different eras and cultures, is in development and set to debut in spring 2024.
Marcus Lee, director of the city's Department of Cultural Affairs, described TimeTravels as streets bustling with period-costumed performers, traditional foods, and crafts.
Isabella Garcia, owner of the café The Modern Roast, expects an influx of visitors to grow local businesses.
Steven Pierce, a public accountant living in the Stonebridge neighborhood, worries that such initiatives dwindle into obscurity because of underfunding or lack of interest.
Leslie Tran, lead architect on the conservancy project, said a phased approach will secure government grants, private sponsorships, and community fundraisers for a stable financial base.
Tech startups have teamed with historians to develop augmented reality tours of historic sites, and local universities involve students in conservation efforts.
Emma Clarkson, a tech entrepreneur and history buff, demonstrated a prototype app that overlays views of how a street looked a century ago.
James Holloway, a retired schoolteacher and local historian, lives in a Victorian house next to the historic Wentworth Manor and supports preservation to teach future generations.
Cheryl Washington, a ceramic artist, supports the SOS Initiative and stresses losing intangible heritage when historic places decay.
Ava Richardson, a seventh-grader at Lincoln Middle School, is excited about touching bricks laid over a hundred years ago.
